tldr: By simultaneously optimizing contact forces and next footstep locations online within a single iLQR-MPC and pairing it with a high-speed whole-body controller, the authors achieved robust bipedal walking capable of withstanding intense disturbance pushes using purely model-based control.
hero_caption: Overall system architecture of the proposed approach. Based on center-of-mass (CoM) targets from high-level reference planning, an iLQR-MPC using a single-rigid-body model simultaneously optimizes contact forces and footstep locations at 100 Hz. A lower-level whole-body controller (WBC) converts these plans into joint torques at 500 Hz, satisfying strict constraints during execution on the robot.
overview:
For bipedal humanoid robots, maintaining balance and continuing to walk when hit by unexpected external pushes is an extremely challenging problem. When strongly pushed, humans prevent falls not only by instantaneously altering the ground reaction force (contact force) under their feet, but also by quickly taking a step to establish a new footstep location. In conventional robot control, however, heavy computational burdens typically led researchers to separate footstep planning from contact force allocation into distinct sequential modules, or to oversimplify contact constraints for convex optimization. As a result, when subjected to large disturbances, robots often slip past friction limits or fail to revise steps in time, leading to falls.

To address this, the authors propose an "iLQR-MPC" based on a single-rigid-body (SRB) model that solves for the contact wrench and footstep locations jointly within a single finite-horizon optimal control problem. By directly embedding the augmented-Lagrangian (AL) method for equality constraints and relaxed-barrier (ReB) penalties for inequality constraints into the backward pass of nonlinear iterative linear-quadratic-regulator (iLQR), the framework strictly respects demanding constraints—such as friction pyramids, zero-moment point (ZMP) stability conditions, and kinematic footstep bounds—while achieving an ultra-fast replanning rate of 100 Hz with a mean solve time of 8.9 ms.

Furthermore, the authors developed a 500 Hz hierarchical whole-body controller (WBC) that reconciles the MPC-planned CoM motion and contact forces with the full-body dynamics of the robot. In MuJoCo simulation experiments using the real-scale humanoid robot Unitree G1, the system demonstrated exceptional recovery performance, instantly stepping out to withstand a 245 N forward impulse and a 175 N lateral impulse during forward walking. The entire framework operates without any reinforcement learning, offering a highly complete model-based control architecture where all behaviors remain interpretable through explicit equations and physical models.
contributions: Formulating a unified framework on a single-rigid-body model that jointly optimizes contact force distribution and footstep locations online within a single iLQR-MPC rather than decoupling them

Integrating the augmented-Lagrangian (AL) method and relaxed-barrier (ReB) penalties into the iLQR backward pass, achieving real-time replanning at 100 Hz (mean 8.9 ms) while satisfying strict contact and geometric constraints
Developing a whole-body controller combining task-priority null-space projection, a dynamics correction QP, and inverse dynamics to map MPC plans into consistent joint torques at 500 Hz

Demonstrating recovery from strong impulsive pushes of 245 N forward and 175 N laterally on the Unitree G1 in simulation without requiring platform-specific policy training like reinforcement learning

sections.heading: Why optimize contact forces and footstep locations simultaneously?
sections.summary: Handling disturbances in humanoid locomotion requires coordinating ankle, hip, and stepping strategies. This section outlines the limitations of simplified MPC and reinforcement learning, and highlights the significance and contributions of jointly solving contact forces and footstep locations in a single iLQR-MPC.
sections.details:
Bipedal robots possess a floating base, high degrees of freedom, and hybrid dynamics where mechanical models switch discontinuously with every footfall. To prevent tipping over, the system must continuously satisfy strict inequality constraints in real time: not only joint torque limits and joint ranges of motion, but also friction cones to prevent foot slipping and ZMP (Zero-Moment Point: the point where the horizontal ground reaction moment is zero) conditions to prevent foot tilting.

In recent years, reinforcement learning with Sim-to-Real transfer has gained popularity. However, it requires extensive training for each individual robot platform and cannot mathematically guarantee safety-critical hard constraints. On the other hand, conventional model-based control relies on a standard hierarchical pipeline combining a low-frequency (50–100 Hz) reduced-order MPC with a high-frequency (500–1000 Hz) whole-body controller (WBC).

Yet, traditional MPC+WBC pipelines suffer from two major shortcomings:
- Failures due to simplified constraints: Over-linearizing models or relaxing constraints for real-time computation can cause the physical robot to exceed friction limits and slip under large disturbances.
- Decoupled footstep and force planning: Most methods decide stepping locations and contact force distributions separately. Consequently, the robot cannot make coordinated, optimal decisions on "how hard to brace while simultaneously relocating the next step" at the instant of a push.

This paper focuses on nonlinear iLQR and integrates augmented-Lagrangian (AL) and relaxed-barrier (ReB) methods, proposing an approach that simultaneously solves for footstep locations and contact forces within the same optimization loop at 100 Hz.

Receiving CoM targets and nominal gait schedules from the high-level reference generator, the iLQR-MPC solves for CoM dynamics, contact wrenches, and optimal footstep locations, which the lower-level WBC maps to joint torques while maintaining kinematic and dynamic feasibility.

sections.heading: Capturing and solving robot motion: the SRB model and iLQR
sections.summary: A single-rigid-body (SRB) model retaining attitude dynamics and full three-axis contact wrenches serves as the internal prediction model for MPC. This section explains the underlying theory of iLQR, which computes optimal feedback control laws rapidly via local quadratic approximations of the nonlinear model.
sections.details:
### II-A System Dynamics Modeling
The prediction model for MPC treats the entire robot as a single rigid body (SRB). Unlike point-mass models such as the LIP, its key advantage is preserving roll, pitch, and yaw 3-axis attitude variations along with the complete relationship of forces and moments (contact wrenches) exerted at the feet.

The state vector $\bm{x}$ includes base orientation angles (Euler angles $\bm{\Phi}$), CoM position $\bm{p}$, angular velocity $\bm{\omega}$, linear velocity $\bm{v}$, and the left and right foot positions $\bm{p}_{i}^f$. The control input $\bm{u}$ consists of contact forces $\bm{F}_i$, contact moments $\bm{\tau}_i$, and foot velocities $\bm{v}_i^f$ for each foot. The dynamics are discretized using forward Euler integration with a sampling period of $\Delta t = 5\,\mathrm{ms}$ and a prediction horizon of $N = 10$ steps (lookahead horizon of $50\,\mathrm{ms}$).

### II-B Solution Framework via iLQR
Iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator (iLQR) is a differential dynamic programming (DDP) family algorithm that converges to a solution by iteratively executing a backward pass (reverse-time computation) and a forward pass (forward-time rollout) while quadratically approximating the nonlinear dynamics and cost around the action-value function $Q_k$. Utilizing the Gauss-Newton approximation, which neglects second-order tensor contractions of the dynamics, drastically reduces computational overhead and simultaneously derives state feedback gain matrices $\bm{K}_k$ and feedforward correction terms $\bm{k}_k$.

sections.heading: Preventing constraint violations: MPC formulation with AL and relaxed barriers
sections.summary: Friction pyramids, ZMP stability constraints, and equality constraints for swing feet are incorporated into the cost function using augmented-Lagrangian (AL) and relaxed-barrier (ReB) methods. This enables fast constrained optimization without disrupting the computational structure of iLQR.
sections.details:
### III-A Contact Stability Constraints
When a foot is in contact with the ground, four physical constraints must strictly hold:
- Unilateral contact constraint permitting only positive vertical normal force ($F_{i,z} \geq 0$)
- Friction pyramid constraint to prevent foot slipping (a 4-sided inner pyramidal approximation of the friction cone)
- ZMP constraint to prevent foot tipping (requiring the ZMP to stay inside the rectangular foot support area $L_x, L_y$)
- Upper and lower bounds on yaw contact moment

These are formulated as linear inequalities on the contact wrench $(\bm{F}_i, \bm{\tau}_i)$. For swing feet, geometric inequality constraints confine the landing location within a bounding box centered around nominal footstep coordinates.

### III-B Embedding Constraints via Penalty Methods
Because iLQR assumes smooth, twice-differentiable cost functions, directly handling hard inequality and equality constraints is difficult. Therefore, the paper strategically selects penalty formulations:
- Augmented-Lagrangian (AL) method: Applied to equality constraints requiring zero contact wrenches during swing phases. Using dual variables $\bm{\lambda}_k$ and penalty parameter $\sigma$, the AL penalty drives constraint violations strictly to zero.
- Relaxed-Barrier (ReB) penalties: Applied to inequality constraints such as friction and ZMP. ReB replaces the standard logarithmic barrier function with a smooth quadratic polynomial near the boundary. This avoids the numerical explosions where barrier functions diverge to infinity and ruin Hessian calculations, dramatically improving the backward pass stability.

### III-C & D Footstep Endogenization and Overall MPC Problem
Foot positions are treated as footstep states within the MPC, updated via gait schedule signals $\gamma_i$ as "fixed if in stance, moved by foot velocity if in swing." Consequently, when disturbed, the robot coordinates "how hard to push with the stance foot" and "where to land the next step" in the exact same single optimization step.

sections.heading: Bridging plans to joint torques: 500 Hz Whole-Body Control (WBC)
sections.summary: Because the CoM motion and contact forces planned by the MPC are based on a reduced-order model, they must be reconciled with the 35-DOF full-body dynamics. This section describes the three-stage whole-body controller operating at 500 Hz: null-space projection, dynamics correction QP, and inverse dynamics.
sections.details:
The objective of the whole-body controller (WBC) is to take MPC plans and compute motor torques for each joint at 500 Hz while strictly accounting for all degrees of freedom (6 floating-base DOFs + 29 joint DOFs = 35 total DOFs for the Unitree G1) and actuator dynamics. It operates in three stages:

### IV-B Null-Space Task-Priority Control
At the highest kinematic level, prioritized target tasks are composed by projecting lower-priority tasks into the null space of higher-priority tasks to avoid interference. Priorities are ordered as: floating-base orientation, foot trajectory, and arm swinging. This yields kinematically consistent nominal joint accelerations $\ddot{\bm{q}}^{\mathrm{kin}}$.

### IV-C Dynamics Correction QP (Quadratic Program)
Accelerations derived purely from kinematics do not yet satisfy floating-base equations of motion or strict contact wrench limits. Thus, a very lightweight QP is solved, containing only 18 decision variables: base acceleration corrections $\delta\ddot{\bm{q}}_f$ (6-dim) and contact wrench corrections $\delta\bm{F}_r$ (12-dim). It satisfies the equations of motion while minimizing corrections to remain as close as possible to MPC targets.

### IV-D Joint Torque Computation and PD Control
Using the dynamically consistent accelerations $\ddot{\bm{q}}^{\mathrm{opt}}$ and contact wrenches $\bm{F}_r^{\mathrm{opt}}$ from the QP, floating-base inverse dynamics are computed directly to uniquely determine feedforward joint torques $\bm{\tau}^{\mathrm{ff}}$. Adding joint-level PD feedback torques produces the final motor torque commands.

sections.heading: Validation on Unitree G1: Steady walking and strong push recovery
sections.summary: Using the physics simulator MuJoCo, walking and disturbance recovery experiments were performed on the humanoid Unitree G1. The robot instantly adapted footstep locations to prevent falls under intense pushes of 245 N forward and 175 N laterally, while the MPC solve time averaged 8.9 ms, confirming real-time feasibility.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations used the MuJoCo simulator and the Unitree G1 model. The WBC and simulation loop ran synchronously at 500 Hz, while the iLQR-MPC replanned every 10 ms (100 Hz) over a 50 ms horizon ($\Delta t = 5\,\mathrm{ms}, N = 10$). Computations ran on a standard desktop CPU (Intel Core i5-12400F).

### V-B Steady-State Walking Performance
During unperturbed flat-ground walking at 0.1 m/s for approximately 40 seconds, MPC predicted trajectories tracked the reference targets with high accuracy. The root-mean-square error (RMSE) for forward position was 0.063 m and vertical error was only 0.001 m, verifying stable gait cycle maintenance.

### V-C Push Recovery Performance
Short 0.12 s impulsive disturbance forces were applied to the robot's torso during walking to test recovery limits.
- Forward pushes ($+x$ direction): The robot sustained pushes up to 245 N while continuing to walk. Upon impact, the pitch angle tilted by roughly 0.20 rad, but the MPC instantly replanned the next footstep forward, settling angular velocity within 1.0 s.
- Lateral pushes ($\pm y$ direction): Pushes from left to right ($-y$ direction) were resisted up to 175 N, whereas right to left ($+y$ direction) capped at 80 N, showing notable asymmetry. This depends on whether the impulse pushed toward the stance foot or toward the swing foot. Pushing toward the stance foot allows bracing via contact wrench redistribution, whereas pushing away from the stance foot narrows the support polygon, leaving stepping as the only recovery option.

### V-D Computational Breakdown
Over approximately 9,000 MPC cycles, the end-to-end mean solve time was only 8.93 ms. A single iLQR iteration took roughly 2.24 ms; while transient disturbance phases peaked at 13.56 ms, the system satisfied the 100 Hz replanning budget across nearly all frames.

captions.F2: Figure 2: MPC prediction and tracking of CoM states during steady walking at 0.1 m/s. Red dashed lines denote reference trajectories, and blue solid lines denote predictions, demonstrating minimal tracking error in both forward position (a) and vertical motion (c).
captions.F3: Figure 3: Recovery response to a 245 N forward (+x) push disturbance. As shown in the snapshot sequence, the robot takes a large step forward to recover, quickly stabilizing pitch angle (a) and angular velocity (d) within approximately 1 second of push onset.
captions.F4: Figure 4: Recovery response to a 175 N lateral (-y) push disturbance. Despite a lateral CoM displacement of roughly 0.34 m (a), the MPC immediately steps outward to suppress roll inclination (b), achieving successful recovery.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: Integrating iLQR-MPC with WBC establishes an interpretable humanoid walking control system with rigorous constraint satisfaction. Future work aims to increase walking speed, incorporate disturbance estimation, and deploy onto real hardware.
sections.details:
This paper presented a model-based control framework integrating an online iLQR-MPC that jointly optimizes contact forces and footstep locations with a hierarchical whole-body controller (WBC) for robust humanoid locomotion. Employing augmented-Lagrangian and relaxed-barrier formulations enabled strict constraint handling within iLQR, demonstrating real-time replanning at 100 Hz.

Nonetheless, the authors identify three primary limitations:
- Walking speed remains relatively modest at 0.1 m/s.
- MPC computation time slightly exceeds the 10 ms cycle budget during transient push phases in some instances.
- Simulation experiments treated disturbance wrenches as known, without an active real-world disturbance estimator.

Future work will focus on achieving higher walking velocities, introducing learned policies for disturbance perception, integrating vision-based footstep planning, and validating the framework on physical Unitree G1 hardware.

takeaways: Jointly solving contact force allocation and footstep locations within a single MPC problem on an SRB model provides exceptional recovery performance against strong disturbance pushes compared to decoupled pipelines.

Combining augmented-Lagrangian (AL) penalties for equality constraints and relaxed-barrier (ReB) penalties for inequality constraints in nonlinear iLQR avoids Hessian divergence and converges rapidly (mean 8.9 ms).
Advancing model-based control architectures (MPC+WBC) enables sophisticated, physically interpretable bipedal locomotion without relying on black-box reinforcement learning.
limitations: Evaluation was limited to a very low walking velocity of 0.1 m/s, leaving robustness against dynamic discrepancies at higher speeds unverified.
During transient disturbance pushes, MPC solve times occasionally exceeded the 10 ms control period (peaking at 13.56 ms).
Simulation experiments assumed disturbance wrenches were known; integration with disturbance observers and state estimators essential for physical hardware remains future work.
